timeline.action: Validate whether the anomaly reflects real runtime CPU saturation.
timeline.observation: processing-service CPU is approximately 392%; memory usage is stable and the container remains running.
timeline.decision_rationale: The OpenSearch signal is confirmed at runtime. More evidence is required to distinguish workload saturation from an application fault.

timeline.action: Inspect recent application logs for exceptions, crash loops or repeated failures.
timeline.observation: No critical application error is present. Processing requests continue successfully while CPU remains saturated.
timeline.decision_rationale: The absence of application errors reduces the likelihood of an exception-driven failure. Workload behaviour should be investigated next.

timeline.action: Retrieve service-specific troubleshooting knowledge for sustained processing CPU saturation.
timeline.observation: The service knowledge base identifies abnormal request volume and CPU-bound processing loops as primary checks when high CPU occurs without memory pressure or error logs.
timeline.decision_rationale: The retrieved runbook supports a workload hypothesis, but current telemetry must confirm that traffic increased.

timeline.action: Correlate CPU behaviour with recent service workload metrics.
timeline.observation: The processing workload increased sharply during the same time window in which CPU rose from the normal baseline to sustained saturation.
timeline.decision_rationale: Metric correlation, healthy memory and the absence of application errors provide sufficient evidence for a workload-induced CPU saturation diagnosis.
timeline.outcome: Evidence threshold reached; investigation can terminate with an explainable diagnosis.

diagnosis.summary: The processing-service is CPU-saturated because of an abnormal increase in processing workload rather than an application crash or memory-related failure.
evidence: Runtime CPU confirmed at approximately 392%, far above the normal baseline.
Memory remained stable during the anomaly.
Recent application logs contained no critical exceptions or crash-loop evidence.
Workload growth was temporally correlated with the CPU increase.
Service-specific RAG documentation identifies workload saturation as the expected troubleshooting path for this signal combination.

alternatives.name: Memory pressure or leak
alternatives.reason: Memory usage remained stable and no memory-pressure evidence was observed.

alternatives.name: Application exception loop
alternatives.reason: No repeated errors or crash-loop messages were present in recent application logs.

remediation.summary: Reduce the abnormal input workload first, verify CPU recovery, and restart processing-service only if saturation persists after workload normalization.

steps.title: Confirm the active CPU saturation
steps.description: From the Windows host, capture the current container resource snapshot before changing the workload.

steps.title: Inspect and reduce the abnormal workload
steps.description: Check the traffic-generator scenario and stop or return it to the normal profile if the increase is not expected.

steps.title: Observe recovery before restarting
steps.description: Wait for the processing queue to drain and confirm that CPU returns close to its learned baseline.

steps.title: Restart only if saturation persists
steps.description: If CPU remains abnormally high after workload normalization, restart processing-service and continue monitoring for recurrence.

verification: processing-service CPU returns close to the normal learned range
request processing remains successful after workload normalization
no new high-grade CPU anomaly is generated by the single-entity detector
application logs remain free of new critical errors
risks: Stopping the traffic generator changes the workload and should be done only when the current traffic increase is not intentional.
Restarting processing-service can interrupt in-flight processing and should remain a secondary action after workload reduction.
